Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Messiah, his character and office.1–3His promises of the future blessedness of the church.4–9The church praises God for these mercies.10, 11
The Spirit-anointed Messiah proclaims good news (verses 1–3)

The prophets sometimes received the Holy Spirit to teach them what to say and move them to proclaim it.

But Jesus Christ possessed the Spirit always and without measure.

As a man, he was thus perfectly equipped for the work the Father had appointed him to accomplish.

People who are materially poor are often more ready to receive the gospel (James 2:5).

Yet the gospel benefits us only when we receive it with humility and meekness.

To those who are poor in spirit, Christ announced good news, as when he pronounced blessing upon the meek.

His atoning satisfaction has been accepted.

Sin's dominion holds us under Satan's power.

But the Son is ready to make us free by his Spirit.

And if the Son makes us free, we are free indeed.

Christ came to destroy sin and Satan, and he triumphed over them through his cross.

Those who stubbornly refuse these invitations will be dealt with as enemies.

Christ was appointed to be a Comforter, and he truly is one.

He comforts all who mourn and look to him rather than to the world for relief.

His purpose is that believers should abound in the fruits of righteousness, like branches planted and tended by God.

God's mercy, Christ's atonement and the gospel of grace do not benefit people who remain proud and self-sufficient.

The Holy Spirit must humble them and show them their true character and needs.

Only then will they recognize their need of the Friend and Savior of sinners.

To people humbled before God, Christ's message is truly glad tidings.

The restored people become God's servants (verses 4–9)

These promises first address Jews returning from captivity.

But they also reach everyone whom grace rescues from spiritual bondage.

An unholy soul resembles a ruined city with broken walls or a destroyed house.

Through the power of Christ's gospel and grace, that soul is restored to become a dwelling place for God through the Spirit.

God's grace can teach us a holy detachment from worldly concerns.

Our hands may remain busy in worldly duties, while our hearts are not entangled in them but remain wholly devoted to God and his service.

Henry connects that detachment with the picture of others carrying out the plowing and vineyard work.

Everyone whom the Lord sets free, he also calls to serve.

Serving God is perfect freedom and the highest honor.

All believers have been made kings and priests to God.

They should therefore live in ways worthy of that calling.

Those who have the Lord as their portion have received an excellent inheritance and should rejoice in it.

The fullness of heavenly joy will more than compensate for everything suffered or given in service.

God loves truth and justice and therefore hates every act of injustice.

Even an offering made to God cannot justify robbery.

Indeed, theft committed under the pretense of making a religious offering is especially hateful.

May the children of godly parents demonstrate the fruit of good instruction, their parents' prayers and the Lord's blessing through the lives they lead.

The redeemed rejoice in salvation (verses 10 and 11)

Only those who are covered now by Christ's righteousness and renewed by the sanctifying Holy Spirit can finally wear the garments of salvation.

Those blessings will spread through future generations as fruit rises from the earth.

With reliable abundance and to the benefit of humanity, God will cause righteousness and praise to grow.

The good news will spread far away, until Christ's salvation is announced to the ends of the earth.

Let us pray earnestly that the Lord will cause this righteousness to grow among us.

It is the true excellence and glory of Christian faith and profession.

[Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3]
Chapter 61
The Messiah, his character and office. ( [Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3] Is. 61:1-3) His promises of the future blessedness of the church. ( [Isa.61.4-Isa.61.9] Is. 61:4-9) The church praises God for these mercies. ( [Isa.61.10] Is. 61:10, [Isa.61.11] 11)
Verses 1-3 The prophets had the Holy Spirit of God at times, teaching them what to say, and causing them to say it; but Christ had the Spirit always, without measure, to qualify him, as man, for the work to which he was appointed. The poor are commonly best disposed to receive the gospel, James 2:5; and it is only likely to profit us when received with meekness. To such as are poor in spirit, Christ preached good tidings when he said, Blessed are the meek. Christ's satisfaction is accepted. By the dominion of sin in us, we are bound under the power of Satan; but the Son is ready, by his Spirit, to make us free; and then we shall be free indeed. Sin and Satan were to be destroyed; and Christ triumphed over them on his cross. But the children of men, who stand out against these offers, shall be dealt with as enemies. Christ was to be a Comforter, and so he is; he is sent to comfort all who mourn, and who seek to him, and not to the world, for comfort. He will do all this for his people, that they may abound in the fruits of righteousness, as the branches of God's planting. Neither the mercy of God, the atonement of Christ, nor the gospel of grace, profit the self-sufficient and proud. They must be humbled, and led to know their own character and wants, by the Holy Spirit, that they may see and feel their need of the sinner's Friend and Saviour. His doctrine contains glad tidings indeed to those who are humbled before God.
[Isa.61.4-Isa.61.9]
Verses 4-9 Promises are here made to the Jews returned out of captivity, which extend to all those who, through grace, are delivered out of spiritual thraldom. An unholy soul is like a city that is broken down, and has no walls, like a house in ruins; but by the power of Christ's gospel and grace, it is fitted to be a habitation of God, through the Spirit. When, by the grace of God, we attain to holy indifference as to the affairs of this world; when, though our hands are employed about them, our hearts are not entangled with them, but preserved entire for God and his service, then the sons of the alien are our ploughmen and vine-dressers. Those whom He sets at liberty, he sets to work. His service is perfect freedom; it is the greatest honour. All believers are made, to our God, kings and priests; and always ought to conduct themselves as such. Those who have the Lord for their portion, have reason to say, that they have worthy portion, and to rejoice in it. In the fulness of heaven's joys we shall receive more than double for all our services and sufferings. God desires truth, and therefore hates all injustice. Nor will it justify any man's robbery to say, it was for burnt-offerings; and that robbery is most hateful which is under this pretence. Let the children of godly parents be such, that all may see the fruits of a good education; an answer to the prayers for them, in the fruit of God's blessing.
[Isa.61.10-Isa.61.11]
Verse 10 ,11 Those only shall be clothed with the garments of salvation hereafter, that are covered with the robe of Christ's righteousness now, and by the sanctification of the Spirit have God's image renewed upon them. These blessings shall spring forth for ages to come, as the fruits of the earth. So duly, so constantly, and with such advantage to mankind, will the Lord God cause righteousness and praise to spring forth. They shall spread far; the great salvation shall be published and proclaimed, to the ends of the earth. Let us be earnest in prayer, that the Lord God may cause that righteousness to spring forth among us, which constitutes the excellence and glory of the Christian profession.

Christ's unchanging love for his church (verses 1–5)

Here the Son of God assures his church of his enduring love and his intercession through all her trials and difficulties.

She will receive a new and pleasant name, different from any name she had before.

Before the gospel was preached widely, hardly anyone seemed sincerely concerned about the true condition of religion in the world.

But by his grace, God has produced something in his church that makes her his delight.

Let that love move us toward holiness.

If the Lord rejoices over us, we should rejoice in serving him.

Ministers and believers persevere in prayer (verses 6–9)

People who profess to belong to God must also be people of prayer.

The Lord is not irritated by earnest pleading, as human beings may be.

He himself tells us to continue crying out and give him no rest.

Jesus' parable of persistent requesting teaches the same principle (Luke 11:5–6).

When God pours out a spirit of prayer on a people, it is a hopeful sign that he is approaching them with mercy.

Notice how uncertain our earthly comforts are.

Notice also God's kindness in granting plenty, together with peace to enjoy it.

May we delight in the gatherings of God's people so that we may experience the consolation of his Spirit.

The way is prepared for salvation (verses 10–12)

God will make a way for Christ's salvation.

Every barrier will be removed.

Christ brings with him the reward of comfort and peace.

But the path before him requires humiliation and reformation.

Those he saves will be called the holy people and the redeemed of the Lord.

Holiness brings honor and beauty to a person or a place.

It makes God's people desirable and loved.

Many historical events may already have fulfilled parts of this promise and served as pledges of more glorious times still to come.

Scripture repeatedly shows the close connection between the blessing of the Jews and that of the Gentiles.

Jesus Christ will finish his work.

He never abandons anyone whom he has redeemed and sanctified.

The victorious Messiah brings judgment (verses 1–6)

In a vision, the prophet sees the Messiah returning in victory from the defeat of his enemies.

Edom serves as a picture of those enemies.

He does not travel as someone worn out by battle.

Rather, he moves in the greatness of his strength, ready to overcome every opposing power.

The Messiah declares that he has been treading the winepress of God's judgment (Revelation 14:19; 19:13).

By his own power, without human assistance, he defeats those stubbornly opposing him.

The appointed day of judgment has come as the time for rescuing his church.

When Christ first appeared on earth, he seemed weak as he poured out his own precious blood in atonement for our sins.

But at the appointed time he will appear in the full display of his strength.

The harvest is rapidly ripening, and the day determined for judgment approaches.

Let sinners seek reconciliation with their righteous Judge before he brings their strength to nothing.

Does Christ say, “I am coming soon”?

Then let our hearts respond, “Come, Lord Jesus; let the time of the redeemed arrive.”

God's mercy remembered amid Israel's rebellion (verses 7–14)

Henry understands the latter part of this chapter and all of the next as expressing, or anticipating, the prayers of Jews at their conversion.

The people remember God's great mercy and favor toward their nation.

They confess their wickedness and stubbornness, ask for pardon and grieve over the long misery they have experienced.

The Father's only Son became the Angel or Messenger of God's love.

He redeemed his people and carried them tenderly.

Yet they complained, resisted the Holy Spirit, despised and persecuted God's prophets, and rejected and crucified the promised Messiah.

Every true comfort and hope we have comes from God's loving-kindness.

Our misery and fears arise from our sins.

Nevertheless, he is the Savior.

When sinners seek the God who in earlier times glorified himself by rescuing, feeding and guiding his purchased flock through danger, they have reason to hope.

He has also given the Holy Spirit to bless his ministers' labors.

Seeking this Savior is a hopeful sign that people are discovering the way of peace.

The church pleads with its everlasting Redeemer (verses 15–19)

The people ask the Lord to look down upon the desolate condition of the nation he once specially favored.

Would it not glorify his name to remove the veil from their hearts and restore the tribes of his inheritance?

The Babylonian captivity and the return that followed were shadows of the greater events predicted here.

God looks upon his people with tenderness and mercy.

Spiritual judgments are more frightening than any outward disaster.

We should avoid the sins that justly cause the Lord to leave people to themselves and to the deceiver.

“Our Redeemer from everlasting” is his name.

His people have always recognized him as the God to whom they could appeal.

The Lord will hear those who belong to him.

He will deliver them from oppression by those who do not bear his name.

Christ's victory over his enemies. ( [Isa.63.1-Isa.63.6] Is. 63:1-6) His mercy toward his church. ( [Isa.63.7-Isa.63.14] Is. 63:7-14) The prayer of the church. ( [Isa.63.15-Isa.63.19] Is. 63:15-19)
Verses 1-6 The prophet, in vision, beholds the Messiah returning in triumph from the conquest of his enemies, of whom Edom was a type. Travelling, not as wearied by the combat, but, in the greatness of his strength, prepared to overcome every opposing power. Messiah declares that he had been treading the wine-press of the wrath of God, Rev. 14:19; 19:13, and by his own power, without any human help, he had crushed his obstinate opposers, for the day of vengeance was determined on, being the appointed season for rescuing his church. Once, he appeared on earth in apparent weakness, to pour out his precious blood as an atonement for our sins; but he will in due time appear in the greatness of his strength. The vintage ripens apace; the day of vengeance, fixed and determined on, approaches apace; let sinners seek to be reconciled to their righteous Judge, ere he brings down their strength to the earth. Does Christ say, "I come quickly?" let our hearts reply, "Even so, come; let the year of the redeemed come."
[Isa.63.7-Isa.63.14]
Verses 7-14 The latter part of this chapter, and the whole of the next, seem to express the prayers of the Jews on their conversation. They acknowledge God's great mercies and favours to their nation. They confess their wickedness and hardness of heart; they entreat his forgiveness, and deplore the miserable condition under which they have so long suffered. The only-begotten Son of the Father became the Angel or Messenger of his love; thus he redeemed and bare them with tenderness. Yet they murmured, and resisted his Holy Spirit, despising and persecuting his prophets, rejecting and crucifying the promised Messiah. All our comforts and hopes spring from the loving-kindness of the Lord, and all our miseries and fears from our sins. But he is the Saviour, and when sinners seek after him, who in other ages glorified himself by saving and feeding his purchased flock, and leading them safely through dangers, and has given his Holy Spirit to prosper the labours of his ministers, there is good ground to hope they are discovering the way of peace.
[Isa.63.15-Isa.63.19]
Verses 15-19 They beseech him to look down on the abject condition of their once-favoured nation. Would it not be glorious to his name to remove the veil from their hearts, to return to the tribes of his inheritance? The Babylonish captivity, and the after-deliverance of the Jews, were shadows of the events here foretold. The Lord looks down upon us in tenderness and mercy. Spiritual judgments are more to be dreaded than any other calamities; and we should most carefully avoid those sins which justly provoke the Lord to leave men to themselves and to their deceiver. "Our Redeemer from everlasting" is thy name; thy people have always looked upon thee as the God to whom they might appeal. The Lord will hear the prayers of those who belong to him, and deliver them from those not called by his name.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe church prays that God's power may be manifested.1–5A confession of sin, and afflictions bewailed.6–12
The church pleads for God to reveal his power (verses 1–5)

God's people long for him to act visibly for them and among them, so that everyone will recognize his power.

This prayer also applies to Christ's second coming, when the Lord himself will descend from heaven.

They appeal to what God has done before and to the kind purposes he has announced for his people.

They need not fear that his promises will disappoint them by failing to come true, because his promises are sure.

Nor will they be disappointed by their fulfillment, because what God provides is completely sufficient.

The happiness of his people rests upon what he has planned and is preparing for them—and upon the way he is preparing them for that blessedness.

It rests on all that God has already done and everything he will yet do.

If we believe this, how could we consider anything too great to expect from his truth, power and love?

The happiness God promises is spiritual, beyond the full comprehension of unaided human understanding.

He stands ready to show grace.

Notice the fellowship between a gracious God and a soul renewed by grace.

We should conscientiously fulfill everything the Lord requires of us.

God meets those who seek to walk in his ways.

This reveals his willingness and eagerness to do them good.

He has been rightly angry with us for our sins.

But that anger is temporary for his reconciled people, whereas his favor is life, continuing and sustaining their salvation.

Confession, helplessness and appeal to the Father (verses 6–12)

In affliction, God's people confess and mourn their sins.

They admit that they have no claim upon his mercy.

Sin is the hateful thing that God opposes.

Whatever outward goodness our deeds seem to possess, if we offer them as a way of earning God's acceptance, they are only rags.

They cannot cover our guilt.

Indeed, they become like filthy rags, making our condition worse.

Even the few good works that really have excellence because they are fruits of the Holy Spirit remain imperfect and stained by the way we carry them out.

They too must be washed in the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness.

It is a dangerous sign when people stop praying.

To pray is to take hold, by faith, of God's promises of good will.

We plead those promises, cling to him and earnestly ask him not to leave us or to return to us when we feel his absence.

The people had brought their trouble on themselves through foolishness.

Sin withers sinners, like something blighted, before the wind of their own wrongdoing carries them away.

When they made themselves unclean, it was no surprise that God regarded them with displeasure.

Yet even in their foolishness, poverty and disgrace they could say:

“You are still our Father.”

The anger they endured was the correction of a Father who could be reconciled to them.

They expected relief from him alone and entrusted their cause to him.

They did not ask, “Lord, do not rebuke us at all.”

Correction might be necessary.

Instead, their plea was, “Do not rebuke us in your displeasure.”

They described their pitiable condition.

See the ruin sin can bring upon a people!

An outward profession of holiness provides no protection against it.

The people did not tell God exactly what to say or do.

They asked him to speak for their comfort and relief.

How few sincerely call upon the Lord or stir themselves up to cling to him!

He may delay the answer to prayer.

But he will finally answer those who call upon his name and hope in his mercy.
classic_reading:
[Isa.64.1-Isa.64.5]
Chapter 64
The church prays that God's power may be manifested. ( [Isa.64.1-Isa.64.5] Is. 64:1-5) A confession of sin, and afflictions bewailed. ( [Isa.64.6-Isa.64.12] Is. 64:6-12)
Verses 1-5 They desire that God would manifest himself to them and for them, so that all may see it. This is applicable to the second coming of Christ, when the Lord himself shall descend from heaven. They plead what God had used to do, and had declared his gracious purpose to do, for his people. They need not fear being disappointed of it, for it is sure; or disappointed in it, for it is sufficient. The happiness of his people is bound up in what God has designed for them, and is preparing for them, and preparing them for; what he has done or will do. Can we believe this, and then think any thing too great to expect from his truth, power, and love? It is spiritual and cannot be comprehended by human understanding. It is ever ready. See what communion there is between a gracious God and a gracious soul. We must make conscience of doing our duty in every thing the Lord our God requires. Thou meetest him; this speaks his freeness and forwardness in doing them good. Though God has been angry with us for our sins, and justly, yet his anger has soon ended; but in his favour is life, which goes on and continues, and on that we depend for our salvation.
[Isa.64.6-Isa.64.12]
Verses 6-12 The people of God, in affliction, confess and bewail their sins, owning themselves unworthy of his mercy. Sin is that abominable thing which the Lord hates. Our deeds, whatever they may seem to be, if we think to merit by them at God's hand, are as rags, and will not cover us; filthy rags, and will but defile us. Even our few good works in which there is real excellence, as fruits of the Spirit, are so defective and defiled as done by us, that they need to be washed in the fountain open for sin and uncleanness. It bodes ill when prayer is kept back. To pray, is by faith to take hold of the promises the Lord has made of his good-will to us, and to plead them; to take hold of him, earnestly begging him not to leave us; or soliciting his return. They brought their troubles upon themselves by their own folly. Sinners are blasted, and then carried away, by the wind of their own iniquity; it withers and then ruins them. When they made themselves as an unclean thing, no wonder that God loathed them. Foolish and careless as we are, poor and despised, yet still Thou art our Father. It is the wrath of a Father we are under, who will be reconciled; and the relief our case requires is expected only from him. They refer themselves to God. They do not say, "Lord, rebuke us not," for that may be necessary; but, "Not in thy displeasure." They state their lamentable condition. See what ruin sin brings upon a people; and an outward profession of holiness will be no defence against it. God's people presume not to tell him what he shall say, but their prayer is, Speak for the comfort and relief of thy people. How few call upon the Lord with their whole hearts, or stir themselves to lay hold upon him! God may delay for a time to answer our prayers, but he will, in the end, answer those who call on his name and hope in his mercy.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe calling of the Gentiles, and the rejection of the Jews.1–7The Lord would preserve a remnant.8–10Judgments upon the wicked.11–16The future happy and flourishing state of the church.17–25
God calls the Gentiles and confronts unbelief (verses 1–7)

The Gentiles began seeking God and found him because he had first sought and found them.

Sometimes the Lord confronts a careless pleasure-seeker or a person openly hostile to him with the words, “Here I am!”

A sudden change follows.

Throughout the gospel age, Christ has waited to show mercy.

But the Jews, though invited, would not come.

Henry therefore says their rejection did not happen without reason.

They insisted on following whatever pleased themselves.

They grieved and resisted the Holy Spirit.

They abandoned God's temple to sacrifice in the groves.

They disregarded the difference between clean and unclean foods before the gospel removed those dietary distinctions.

Henry suggests this behavior may represent all forbidden pleasures and everything people think they will gain through sin—that hateful thing God opposes.

Jesus spoke many warnings against the pride and hypocrisy he encountered.

The charge against such conduct is clear.

We too must watch against pride and preferring ourselves to others.

Every sin, including the most secret thought of the heart, is known to God and will come under his judgment.

The Lord preserves a remnant (verses 8–10)

A cluster of grapes that seems unripe and worthless may still contain new wine.

The Jewish people have continued as a distinct people, providing witness to the fulfillment of ancient promises and prophecies.

God's chosen ones, the spiritual offspring of praying Jacob, will inherit his mountains of happiness and joy.

He will bring them safely there through the valley of tears.

Everything ultimately displays God's glory in the redemption of sinners.

The different ends of faithful and unfaithful people (verses 11–16)

Here the prophet contrasts the godly with the wicked and Jews who believed with those who continued in unbelief.

The wicked spread a table for a host of pagan deities and poured out offerings to the many false gods.

Those worshipers were willing to spend generously for their idols.

This should shame people who claim to worship the true God while begrudging his service.

See how malicious sin really is.

It means choosing to do what we know displeases God.

In every nation and age, the Lord leaves people who persist in wrongdoing and despise his gospel's call to face the consequences.

But his servants receive the bread of life and will lack nothing truly good for them.

Those abandoning God will be ashamed of their false confidence in their own righteousness and the hopes built upon it.

Worldly people congratulate themselves over possessions and prosperity.

God's servants rejoice in God himself.

He is their strength and their portion.

They honor him as the God of truth.

He promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him.

His people count themselves happy to belong to the God who has made them forget their troubles.

The promised new creation and peace (verses 17–25)

Through the grace and comfort believers receive from Jesus Christ, we should understand the promise of a new heaven and a new earth.

The earlier disorder, sin and misery of humanity will no longer be remembered or repeated.

The prophet describes the coming happiness of the church through many images.

A person who dies at a hundred years old will be regarded as dying young; such long life will be expected.

Henry explicitly leaves the precise fulfillment open, saying that only events will determine what these images mean.

Nevertheless, he reasons that if Christianity became universal, the decline of violence and evil could greatly extend human life.

During those blessed times, God's people will enjoy the fruits of their labor.

Children will no longer bring misery to their parents or endure misery themselves.

Sinful dispositions will be completely brought under control, and everyone will live in harmony.

The church on earth will enjoy a happiness resembling heaven.

This prophecy assures Christ's servants that a time is approaching when they will enjoy undisturbed all that they need for true happiness.

As God's fellow workers, let us attend his ordinances and obey his commands.

And it was promised that in him should all the families of the earth be blessed. They shall think themselves happy in having him for their God, who made them forget their troubles.
[Isa.65.17-Isa.65.25]
Verses 17-25 In the grace and comfort believers have in and from Christ, we are to look for this new heaven and new earth. The former confusions, sins and miseries of the human race, shall be no more remembered or renewed. The approaching happy state of the church is described under a variety of images. He shall be thought to die in his youth, and for his sins, who only lives to the age of a hundred years. The event alone can determine what is meant; but it is plain that Christianity, if universal, would so do away violence and evil, as greatly to lengthen life. In those happy days, all God's people shall enjoy the fruit of their labours. Nor will children then be the trouble of their parents, or suffer trouble themselves. The evil dispositions of sinners shall be completely moritified; all shall live in harmony. Thus the church on earth shall be full of happiness, like heaven. This prophecy assures the servants of Christ, that the time approaches, wherein they shall be blessed with the undisturbed enjoyment of all that is needful for their happiness. As workers together with God, let us attend his ordinances, and obey his commands.

This is a prophetic announcement of the Lord's judgment upon those who oppose his church.

Henry applies it especially to what he calls antichristian opponents of the gospel in the last days.

These expressions are figurative, pointing to the many gracious helps God provides for bringing his chosen people home to Christ.

A gospel ministry will be established among the gathered people, with solemn worship before the Lord.

The final verse portrays the punishment of sinners in the world to come.

Jesus himself applied this imagery to the everlasting misery of those who continue without repentance.

Chapter 66
God looks at the heart, and vengeance is threatened for guilt. ( [Isa.66.1-Isa.66.4] Is. 66:1-4) The increase of the church, when Jew and Gentile shall be gathered to the Redeemer. ( [Isa.66.5-Isa.66.14] Is. 66:5-14) Every enemy of the church shall be destroyed, and the final ruin of ungodly men shall be seen. ( [Isa.66.15-Isa.66.24] Is. 66:15-24)
Verses 1-4 The Jews gloried much in their temple. But what satisfaction can the Eternal Mind take in a house made with men's hands? God has a heaven and an earth of his own making, and temples of man's making; but he overlooks them, that he may look with favour to him who is poor in spirit and serious, self-abasing and self-denying; whose heart truly sorrows for sin: such a heart is a living temple for God. The sacrifice of the wicked is not only unacceptable, but a great offence to God. And he that now offers a sacrifice after the law, does in effect set aside Christ's sacrifice. He that burns incense, puts contempt upon the incense of Christ's intercession, and is as if he blessed an idol. Men shall be deceived by the vain confidences with which they deceive themselves. Unbelieving hearts, and unpurified consciences, need no more to make them miserable, than to have their own fears brought upon them. Whatever men put in the place of the priesthood, atonement, and intercession of Christ, will be found hateful to God.
[Isa.66.5-Isa.66.14]
Verses 5-14 The prophet turns to those that trembled at God's word, to comfort and encourage them. The Lord will appear, to the joy of the humble believer, and to the confusion of hypocrites and persecutors. When the Spirit was poured out, and the gospel went forth from Zion, multitudes were converted in a little time. The word of God, especially his promises, and ordinances, are the consolations of the church. The true happiness of all Christians is increased by every convert brought to Christ. The gospel brings with it, wherever it is received in its power, such a river of peace, as will carry us to the ocean of boundless and endless bliss. Divine comforts reach the inward man; the joy of the Lord will be the strength of the believer. Both God's mercy and justice shall be manifested, and for ever magnified.
[Isa.66.15-Isa.66.24]
Verses 15-24 A prophetic declaration is given of the Lord's vengeance on all enemies of his church, especially that of all antichristian opposers of the gospel in the latter days. [Isa.66.19] Is. 66:19, [Isa.66.20] 20, set forth the abundance of means for conversion of sinners. These expressions are figurative, and express the plentiful and gracious helps for bringing God's elect home to Christ. All shall be welcome; and nothing shall be wanting for their assistance and encouragement. A gospel ministry shall be set up in the church; they would have solemn worship before the Lord. In the last verse the nature of the punishment of sinners in the world to come is represented. Then shall the righteous and wicked be separated. Our Saviour applies this to the everlasting misery and torment of impenitent sinners in the future state. To the honour of that free grace which thus distinguishes them, let the redeemed of the Lord, with humility, and not without holy trembling, sing triumphant songs. With this affecting representation of the opposite states of the righteous and wicked, characters which include the whole human race, Isaiah concludes his prophecies. May God grant, for Christ's sake, that our portion may be with those who fear and love his name, who cleave to his truths, and persevere in every good work, looking to receive from the Lord Jesus Christ the gracious invitation, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
